In [Lesson 6](lesson6.qmd) you estimated a single adjusted prevalence ratio (PR) for tree canopy and
high blood pressure: **0.71**, adjusted for education and tract poverty. That one number assumes the
association is the same for everyone in the study. This lesson asks whether it **differs across
groups** — that is, whether a third variable is an **effect modifier**. We use **gender** as the
example. The lesson has two parts:

1. **Stratified analysis** — fitting the adjusted model separately for men and for women, comparing
   the two estimates by eye, and testing the difference with **Cochran's Q**.
2. **Interaction models** — fitting a single model with an **exposure × modifier** interaction term,
   getting stratum-specific estimates from it, and testing the interaction with a **Wald test** and a
   **likelihood ratio test (LRT)**.

The lesson ends with a **🧠 Your Turn** for the exposure and outcome in your own project. It
produces a first draft of the stratified results table and interaction tests that Milestone 4 asks
for (and that become **Table 3** of your final report).

# Setup

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)
library(sandwich)
```

In RStudio:

```r
data <- read.csv(file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"))
```

In the browser:

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true

data_base_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/schinasi/EOH635/main/data/"

dir.create("data_processed", showWarnings = FALSE)

download.file(paste0(data_base_url, "class_data_processed.csv"), file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"))

data <- read.csv(file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## 💻 In your RStudio script

```r
data <- read.csv(file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"))
```
:::

Recreate the variables from earlier lessons — the cleaned age variable (Lesson 3) and the
top-quartile tree canopy exposure (Lesson 5) — and the `extract_ratio()` helper from Lesson 6.

```{webr-r}
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    r_age = ifelse(age > 105, NA, age),                       # Lesson 3: implausible ages -> missing
    tree_quartile = factor(ntile(hrlctree, 4)),               # Lesson 5: canopy quartiles
    tree_top_quartile = ifelse(tree_quartile == "4", 1, 0)    # Lesson 5: Q4 (1) vs. Q1-Q3 (0)
  )

# Lesson 6 helper: exponentiated coefficients and 95% CIs (robust = TRUE for modified Poisson)
extract_ratio <- function(model, label, robust = FALSE) {
  vc <- if (robust) vcovHC(model, type = "HC0") else vcov(model)
  b  <- coef(model)[-1]
  se <- sqrt(diag(vc))[-1]
  data.frame(Model = label, Term = names(b), Estimate = exp(b),
             CI_Lower = exp(b - 1.96 * se), CI_Upper = exp(b + 1.96 * se),
             row.names = NULL)
}
```

And here is where Lesson 6 ended — the final adjusted model, fit with modified Poisson regression:

```{webr-r}
model_final <- glm(high_blood_pressure ~ tree_top_quartile + education + pov_allage,
                   data = data, family = poisson(link = "log"))

extract_ratio(model_final, "Adjusted for education and tract poverty", robust = TRUE) %>%
  filter(Term == "tree_top_quartile")
```

**PR = 0.71 (95% CI: 0.58, 0.86).** This lesson asks: is that 0.71 a good summary for *everyone*, or
is the association different for men and for women?

---

# Effect Modification vs. Confounding

Before any code, keep the distinction from Lessons 6 and 7 clear:

| | Confounding | Effect modification |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A **bias**: a third variable distorts the exposure–outcome association | A **finding**: the association really is different in different groups |
| What we do about it | **Remove** it (adjust, using the DAG) | **Describe and report** it (stratify, test) |
| Question it answers | "Is the overall estimate distorted?" | "Is one overall estimate the right summary?" |

The same variable can be a confounder, an effect modifier, both, or neither. Education was a
confounder in Lesson 6; whether it is also a modifier is a separate question.

Effect modification also depends on the **scale**. An association can differ across groups on the
**multiplicative** (ratio) scale but not the **additive** (difference) scale, or vice versa. Our
models estimate PRs, so the formal tests in this lesson are tests of **multiplicative**
interaction. Step 3 shows both scales for the crude data.

---

# Part 1: Stratified Analysis

## Step 1: State your hypothesis first

Effect modification analyses are easy to over-interpret, because with enough subgroups *something*
will look different by chance. The protection is the same as for confounding in Lesson 6: **decide
in advance** which modifier you will examine, what you expect, and what threshold you will use.

For this lesson, we write down the following before looking at the data:

> *A priori hypothesis:* The association between tree canopy and high blood pressure will differ by
> gender. Men and women can differ in how much time they spend in their neighborhood, how they use
> green space (e.g., for physical activity), and in their risk of high blood pressure, so the benefit
> of tree canopy may not be the same for both. We will consider a p-value below **0.10** from a test
> of interaction to be statistical evidence of effect modification.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why 0.10 and not 0.05?

Tests of interaction compare *two* estimates, each with its own uncertainty, so they have much less
statistical power than a test of the main association. A higher threshold (commonly 0.10, sometimes
0.15 or 0.20) reduces the chance of missing real effect modification (a type II error). Like the 10%
rule in Lesson 6, this is a convention: choose it before you look, report it, and don't move it after
you see the results.
:::

## Step 2: Code the modifier and check the cell sizes

```{webr-r}
table(data$gender, useNA = "ifany")
```

There are three gender categories, and two participants are missing gender. Before deciding how to
code the modifier, check how many participants fall in each combination of **modifier ×
exposure × outcome** — these are the people who carry the information in each stratum.

```{webr-r}
data %>%
  filter(!is.na(gender)) %>%
  count(gender, tree_top_quartile, high_blood_pressure) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = high_blood_pressure, values_from = n,
              names_prefix = "high_bp_")
```

**Questions to consider:**

- How many non-binary participants live in a top-quartile canopy tract **and** have high blood
  pressure?
- What would happen if you tried to estimate a PR for tree canopy among non-binary participants?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Answers — click to reveal after you've thought about it"}
- **One.** Of the 26 non-binary participants, 6 live in a top-quartile tract, and 1 of those 6 has
  high blood pressure.
- A PR based on one or two cases would have an extremely wide confidence interval (or the model
  might not converge at all), so it would tell us almost nothing.

We have two options: exclude non-binary participants from the effect modification analysis, or
combine them with another group. Combining only makes sense if we have reason to believe their
association is similar to that group's — and we have no basis for that. So, as in the original
version of this course, **we exclude the 26 non-binary participants from the effect modification
analysis** (they remain in the overall analyses), and we note this as a limitation: the study cannot
say anything about the association among non-binary people.
:::

Code gender as a **0/1 numeric variable**. A 0/1 coding makes the interaction model in Part 2 much
easier to read.

```{webr-r}
data <- data %>%
  mutate(woman = case_when(gender == "Woman" ~ 1,
                           gender == "Man"   ~ 0,
                           TRUE              ~ NA_real_))   # non-binary and missing -> NA

table(data$gender, data$woman, useNA = "ifany")   # always check a recode
```

Last, create the **analytic sample**: participants with no missing data on the outcome, exposure,
modifier, or adjustment variables. Every model in this lesson uses `data_em`, so every comparison is
made in the same people — the same rule as the change-in-estimate approach in Lesson 6.

```{webr-r}
data_em <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(high_blood_pressure), !is.na(tree_top_quartile), !is.na(woman),
         !is.na(education), !is.na(pov_allage))

nrow(data_em)
table(data_em$woman, data_em$tree_top_quartile)
```

## Step 3: Look at the four groups

Before fitting any models, look at the prevalence of high blood pressure in each of the four
combinations of gender and exposure.

```{webr-r}
four_groups <- data_em %>%
  group_by(woman, tree_top_quartile) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), prevalence = mean(high_blood_pressure), .groups = "drop")

four_groups

# Within each gender: the crude PR (ratio scale) and prevalence difference (additive scale)
four_groups %>%
  group_by(woman) %>%
  summarise(
    PR = prevalence[tree_top_quartile == 1] / prevalence[tree_top_quartile == 0],
    PD_percentage_points = 100 * (prevalence[tree_top_quartile == 1] - prevalence[tree_top_quartile == 0])
  )
```

**Questions to consider:**

- Among men, how does the prevalence of high blood pressure compare in top-quartile vs. other tracts?
  Among women?
- On the ratio scale, is the crude association stronger in men or in women? On the additive scale?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Answers — click to reveal after you've thought about it"}
- **Men:** 18.1% in top-quartile tracts vs. 36.1% elsewhere. **Women:** 22.1% vs. 32.3%.
- On the **ratio** scale, the crude PR is **0.50** for men and **0.69** for women — a stronger
  (further from 1) association among men. On the **additive** scale, the prevalence difference is
  **−17.9 percentage points** for men and **−10.2** for women — also stronger among men. Here the two
  scales agree on the direction of the difference; they don't always. These are **crude** numbers;
  the next step adjusts for the confounders from Lesson 6.
:::

## Step 4: Fit the adjusted model within each stratum

A **stratified analysis** fits the same adjusted model separately in each level of the modifier.
Within each stratum, gender is constant, so it drops out of the model; the adjustment set from
Lesson 6 (education and tract poverty) stays in.

```{webr-r}
model_men <- glm(high_blood_pressure ~ tree_top_quartile + education + pov_allage,
                 data = filter(data_em, woman == 0), family = poisson(link = "log"))

model_women <- glm(high_blood_pressure ~ tree_top_quartile + education + pov_allage,
                   data = filter(data_em, woman == 1), family = poisson(link = "log"))

stratified <- bind_rows(
  extract_ratio(model_men, "Men", robust = TRUE),
  extract_ratio(model_women, "Women", robust = TRUE)
) %>%
  filter(Term == "tree_top_quartile") %>%                # keep the exposure only
  mutate(N = c(nobs(model_men), nobs(model_women)))

stratified %>% mutate(across(Estimate:CI_Upper, ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

We keep only the `tree_top_quartile` rows: the PRs for education and tract poverty are there to
adjust the exposure estimate, not to be interpreted (the "Table 2 fallacy" from Lesson 6).

A plot makes the comparison easier to see. Note the **log scale** on the y-axis: ratios should be
plotted on a log scale, so that, for example, 0.5 and 2.0 are the same distance from 1.

```{webr-r}
ggplot(stratified, aes(x = Model, y = Estimate, ymin = CI_Lower, ymax = CI_Upper)) +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Adjusted PR (95% CI), log scale",
       title = "Tree canopy (top quartile vs. rest) and high blood pressure, by gender") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Step 5: Qualitative assessment — compare the estimates by eye

Two questions guide a qualitative assessment:

1. **Are the point estimates meaningfully different?** Is the difference large enough to matter for
   public health, regardless of p-values?
2. **How much do the confidence intervals overlap?** Substantial overlap — especially if one
   stratum's point estimate falls inside the other's CI — suggests weak evidence of a difference.
   Little or no overlap suggests a difference that is unlikely to be due to chance alone.

**Questions to consider:**

- Interpret the PR for men and the PR for women, each in one sentence.
- Do the confidence intervals overlap? Does either point estimate fall inside the other CI?
- The CI for men excludes 1 and the CI for women includes 1. Does that mean the association is
  "significant in men but not in women," and therefore that gender modifies the association?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Answers — click to reveal after you've thought about it"}
| Gender | N | Adjusted PR (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|
| Men | 933 | 0.62 (0.45, 0.84) |
| Women | 1,027 | 0.81 (0.62, 1.05) |

- *Men:* After adjusting for education and tract poverty, the prevalence of high blood pressure among
  men living in the greenest quarter of census tracts was 0.62 times the prevalence among men living
  in the other three quarters (95% CI: 0.45, 0.84) — about 38% lower. *Women:* the corresponding PR
  was 0.81 (95% CI: 0.62, 1.05) — about 19% lower.
- Yes, substantially. The women's point estimate (0.81) falls inside the men's CI (0.45–0.84), and
  the men's point estimate (0.62) sits right at the lower edge of the women's CI (0.62–1.05). The
  difference in point estimates is suggestive, but this much overlap means it could easily be due to
  chance.
- **No.** This is one of the most common mistakes in effect modification analysis (see this week's
  Kaufman & MacLehose reading). "Significant in one group, not in the other" is not a test of whether
  the two estimates *differ from each other*. The women's CI includes 1 partly because the estimate is
  smaller, but both CIs point in the same, protective direction. To test whether the two estimates
  differ, we need a formal test of heterogeneity — Steps 6 through 9.
:::

## Step 6: Cochran's Q — a test of heterogeneity across strata

**Cochran's Q** tests whether stratum-specific estimates differ more than we would expect by chance.
It needs only the estimate and its standard error from each stratum, so it can be used with any
stratified estimates — including ones from published papers. Because ratio estimates are
approximately normal on the **log** scale, Q is calculated with the log PRs:

$$Q = \sum_i w_i \left(\ln \text{PR}_i - \ln \text{PR}_{\text{pooled}}\right)^2, \qquad w_i = \frac{1}{SE_i^2}, \qquad \ln \text{PR}_{\text{pooled}} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \ln \text{PR}_i}{\sum_i w_i}$$

- $\ln \text{PR}_i$ is the log PR in stratum $i$, and $SE_i$ is its standard error;
- the pooled estimate is a weighted average, giving more weight to more precise strata;
- under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity, Q follows a chi-square distribution with
  (number of strata − 1) degrees of freedom.

```{webr-r}
# Log PRs and robust SEs for tree canopy, from each stratum
log_pr <- c(coef(model_men)["tree_top_quartile"],
            coef(model_women)["tree_top_quartile"])
se     <- c(sqrt(vcovHC(model_men,   type = "HC0")["tree_top_quartile", "tree_top_quartile"]),
            sqrt(vcovHC(model_women, type = "HC0")["tree_top_quartile", "tree_top_quartile"]))

w <- 1 / se^2                                    # inverse-variance weights
log_pr_pooled <- sum(w * log_pr) / sum(w)        # weighted average
Q  <- sum(w * (log_pr - log_pr_pooled)^2)
df <- length(log_pr) - 1
p_Q <- pchisq(Q, df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)

c(pooled_PR = exp(log_pr_pooled), Q = Q, df = df, p_value = p_Q)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Only have the PR and its 95% CI? Click to see how to get the SE"}
A 95% CI on the log scale is $\ln \text{PR} \pm 1.96 \times SE$, so its total width is
$2 \times 1.96 \times SE = 3.92 \times SE$. To recover the SE from a published PR and CI:

$$SE = \frac{\ln(\text{upper limit}) - \ln(\text{lower limit})}{3.92}$$

```{webr-r}
(log(stratified$CI_Upper) - log(stratified$CI_Lower)) / 3.92   # same as `se` above
```

Always work on the **log** scale. Calculating Q or the SE from the PRs themselves (without taking
logs) gives the wrong answer.
:::

**Questions to consider:**

- What is the p-value for Cochran's Q? Using our pre-specified threshold of 0.10, is there
  statistical evidence of heterogeneity?
- Why might Q fail to detect a real difference here?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Answers — click to reveal after you've thought about it"}
- **Q = 1.70, 1 df, p = 0.19.** That is above 0.10, so there is no statistical evidence of
  heterogeneity by this test.
- Q has **low power** when there are few strata and each estimate is imprecise — exactly our
  situation (two strata, wide CIs). A p-value of 0.19 does **not** show that the association is the
  same in men and women; it shows the data can't rule out a difference of this size arising by chance.
:::

---

# Part 2: Interaction Models

## Step 7: Fit a model with an interaction term

Instead of fitting separate models, we can fit **one** model that includes the exposure, the
modifier, and their product — an **interaction term**:

$$\ln(\text{prevalence}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{TreeTop} + \beta_2\,\text{Woman} + \beta_3\,(\text{TreeTop} \times \text{Woman}) + \beta_4\,\text{Education} + \beta_5\,\text{TractPoverty}$$

In R, `tree_top_quartile * woman` is shorthand for `tree_top_quartile + woman +
tree_top_quartile:woman` — both **main effects** plus their interaction.

```{webr-r}
model_int <- glm(high_blood_pressure ~ tree_top_quartile * woman + education + pov_allage,
                 data = data_em, family = poisson(link = "log"))

V_int <- vcovHC(model_int, type = "HC0")    # robust variance-covariance matrix

data.frame(
  estimate  = coef(model_int),
  robust_se = sqrt(diag(V_int))
) %>% round(3)
```

What each coefficient means (everything holds education and tract poverty constant):

| Coefficient | Term | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $\beta_1$ | `tree_top_quartile` | Log PR for tree canopy **among men** (woman = 0) |
| $\beta_2$ | `woman` | Log PR for women vs. men **in tracts outside the top quartile** |
| $\beta_3$ | `tree_top_quartile:woman` | How much the log PR for tree canopy **differs** in women compared with men |
| $\beta_1 + \beta_3$ | | Log PR for tree canopy **among women** (woman = 1) |

Where does $\beta_1 + \beta_3$ come from? Write out the model for women (Woman = 1) in top-quartile
and other tracts, and subtract:

- Top quartile: $\beta_0 + \beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 + \ldots$
- Other tracts: $\beta_0 + \beta_2 + \ldots$
- Difference: $\beta_1 + \beta_3$ (everything else cancels)

For men (Woman = 0), the $\beta_2$ and $\beta_3$ terms are multiplied by 0, so the difference is just
$\beta_1$.

## Step 8: Stratum-specific estimates from the interaction model

The PR for men is $e^{\beta_1}$, and the PR for women is $e^{\beta_1 + \beta_3}$. The CI for women
needs the variance of a **sum** of two coefficients, which includes their covariance:

$$\text{Var}(\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3) = \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) + \text{Var}(\hat\beta_3) + 2\,\text{Cov}(\hat\beta_1, \hat\beta_3)$$

```{webr-r}
b1 <- coef(model_int)["tree_top_quartile"]
b3 <- coef(model_int)["tree_top_quartile:woman"]

se_men   <- sqrt(V_int["tree_top_quartile", "tree_top_quartile"])
se_women <- sqrt(V_int["tree_top_quartile", "tree_top_quartile"] +
                 V_int["tree_top_quartile:woman", "tree_top_quartile:woman"] +
                 2 * V_int["tree_top_quartile", "tree_top_quartile:woman"])

data.frame(
  Stratum  = c("Men", "Women"),
  PR       = exp(c(b1, b1 + b3)),
  CI_Lower = exp(c(b1 - 1.96 * se_men, b1 + b3 - 1.96 * se_women)),
  CI_Upper = exp(c(b1 + 1.96 * se_men, b1 + b3 + 1.96 * se_women)),
  row.names = NULL
) %>% mutate(across(PR:CI_Upper, ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

**Questions to consider:**

- How do these PRs compare with the stratified PRs from Step 4? Why aren't they identical?
- What is $e^{\beta_3}$, and how would you put it into words?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Answers — click to reveal after you've thought about it"}
- From the interaction model: men **0.61 (0.45, 0.82)**, women **0.82 (0.63, 1.06)**. From the
  stratified models: men 0.62 (0.45, 0.84), women 0.81 (0.62, 1.05). They are very close but not
  identical, because the interaction model lets only the **tree canopy** association differ by gender —
  it assumes the associations of education and tract poverty with high blood pressure are the same
  for men and women. The stratified models let *every* coefficient differ. Either approach is
  acceptable; say which one you used.
- $e^{\beta_3} = e^{0.300} = $ **1.35** — the **ratio of the two PRs** (0.82 / 0.61 ≈ 1.35). The PR
  for tree canopy among women is 1.35 times the PR among men; that is, the association is weaker
  (closer to 1) among women. If there were no multiplicative interaction, $\beta_3$ would be 0 and
  $e^{\beta_3}$ would be 1.
:::

## Step 9: Testing the interaction — the Wald test

The **Wald test** asks whether the interaction coefficient is different from zero:

$$z = \frac{\hat\beta_3}{SE(\hat\beta_3)}$$

Compare $z$ with a standard normal distribution. For a modified Poisson model, use the **robust**
standard error.

```{webr-r}
se_b3 <- sqrt(V_int["tree_top_quartile:woman", "tree_top_quartile:woman"])
z_wald <- b3 / se_b3
p_wald <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_wald))

c(beta3 = unname(b3), robust_se = se_b3, z = unname(z_wald), p_value = unname(p_wald))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Don't read the Wald p-value from `summary()` for a modified Poisson model

`summary(model_int)` also prints a z value and p-value for every coefficient, but those use the
**model-based** Poisson standard errors, which are wrong for a 0/1 outcome (Lesson 6, Step 4). Here
`summary()` gives p = 0.18; the correct, robust Wald test gives p = 0.12. Always use the robust SE
for modified Poisson models.
:::

## Step 10: Testing the interaction — the likelihood ratio test

The **likelihood ratio test (LRT)** compares how well two **nested** models fit the data:

- a **reduced** model, *without* the interaction term: `exposure + modifier + covariates`
- a **full** model, *with* it: `exposure * modifier + covariates`

$$\text{LRT statistic} = -2 \times \left(\ln L_{\text{reduced}} - \ln L_{\text{full}}\right) \sim \chi^2_{df}$$

where $\ln L$ is each model's log-likelihood, and $df$ is the number of parameters added in the full
model (1 for a single interaction term).

::: {.callout-important}
## Use a model with a real likelihood for the LRT

An LRT compares **likelihoods**, so the likelihood has to be the right one for the data. A modified
Poisson model uses the Poisson likelihood, which is the *wrong* likelihood for a 0/1 outcome — that is
exactly why it needs robust standard errors. So for a binary outcome, run the LRT on **log-binomial**
models (if they converge), which estimate the same PR with the correct likelihood. If your
log-binomial models won't converge, rely on the robust Wald test (Step 9), plus Cochran's Q.
:::

Our log-binomial models converge here, so we use them:

```{webr-r}
model_reduced_lb <- glm(high_blood_pressure ~ tree_top_quartile + woman + education + pov_allage,
                        data = data_em, family = binomial(link = "log"))
model_full_lb    <- glm(high_blood_pressure ~ tree_top_quartile * woman + education + pov_allage,
                        data = data_em, family = binomial(link = "log"))

# The LRT by hand
ll_reduced <- logLik(model_reduced_lb)
ll_full    <- logLik(model_full_lb)

lrt_stat <- -2 * (as.numeric(ll_reduced) - as.numeric(ll_full))
lrt_df   <- attr(ll_full, "df") - attr(ll_reduced, "df")      # number of added parameters
p_lrt    <- pchisq(lrt_stat, df = lrt_df, lower.tail = FALSE)

c(logLik_reduced = as.numeric(ll_reduced), logLik_full = as.numeric(ll_full),
  LRT = lrt_stat, df = lrt_df, p_value = p_lrt)

# The same test in one line
anova(model_reduced_lb, model_full_lb, test = "Chisq")
```

In the `anova()` output, `Deviance` in the second row is the LRT statistic, `Df` is its degrees of
freedom, and `Pr(>Chi)` is the p-value.

Two rules keep an LRT valid:

1. **The models must be nested.** The reduced model contains *everything* in the full model except
   the interaction term — including the modifier's main effect. Comparing `outcome ~ exposure` with
   `outcome ~ exposure * modifier` tests two parameters at once (the modifier's main effect and the
   interaction), which is not a test of effect modification.
2. **Both models must be fit in the same participants.** If the modifier has missing values and the
   reduced model doesn't include it, R will fit the two models in different people, and the
   comparison is meaningless. Fitting both models in `data_em` prevents this.

```{webr-r}
# The trap in rule 2: a reduced model without `woman`, fit in the full dataset
model_wrong_reduced <- glm(high_blood_pressure ~ tree_top_quartile + education + pov_allage,
                           data = data, family = binomial(link = "log"))

c(N_wrong_reduced = nobs(model_wrong_reduced), N_full = nobs(model_full_lb))
```

The two models use different numbers of participants (the 26 non-binary participants and those
missing gender are in one but not the other). `anova()` will refuse to compare them, or, in some
situations, compare them silently with a meaningless result.

**Questions to consider:**

- What are the Wald and LRT p-values? Using our pre-specified threshold of 0.10, what do you conclude?
- Would your conclusion change with a threshold of 0.15? What does that tell you about choosing the
  threshold in advance?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Answers — click to reveal after you've thought about it"}
- **Robust Wald test: z = 1.54, p = 0.12.** **LRT (log-binomial): statistic = 2.20, 1 df,
  p = 0.14.** Both are above 0.10, so by our pre-specified rule there is **no statistical evidence**
  of multiplicative effect modification by gender. Cochran's Q (p = 0.19) agrees.
- With a 0.15 threshold, both the Wald test and the LRT would count as evidence of modification. The
  data are the same; only the rule changed. That is why the threshold must be chosen **before** you
  see the results. Choosing it afterward to get the answer you want is a form of p-hacking. Whatever
  the threshold, report the actual p-values so readers can judge for themselves.
:::

## Step 11: Keep the model hierarchical

When a model contains an interaction term, it must also contain **both main effects** that make up
the interaction. This is the **hierarchy principle**. Here is what happens if the main effect of
gender is left out:

```{webr-r}
model_nonhier <- glm(high_blood_pressure ~ tree_top_quartile + tree_top_quartile:woman +
                       education + pov_allage,
                     data = data_em, family = poisson(link = "log"))

bind_rows(
  extract_ratio(model_int, "Hierarchical (correct)", robust = TRUE),
  extract_ratio(model_nonhier, "Missing main effect of woman", robust = TRUE)
) %>%
  filter(Term %in% c("tree_top_quartile", "woman", "tree_top_quartile:woman")) %>%
  mutate(across(Estimate:CI_Upper, ~ round(.x, 2)))
```

Without the `woman` main effect, the model assumes that women and men in tracts outside the top
quartile have *exactly the same* prevalence of high blood pressure. The interaction term then soaks
up part of the difference between women and men, so it no longer measures only how the tree canopy
association differs by gender (here it shrinks from 1.35 to 1.22). Writing `exposure * modifier`
always includes both main effects for you.

## Step 12: Put it together — a results table and interpretation

Effect modification results are usually presented as a table of stratum-specific estimates with the
test(s) of interaction — **Table 3** of your final report:

```{webr-r}
overall <- extract_ratio(
  glm(high_blood_pressure ~ tree_top_quartile + education + pov_allage,
      data = data_em, family = poisson(link = "log")),
  "Overall", robust = TRUE) %>%
  filter(Term == "tree_top_quartile") %>%
  mutate(N = nrow(data_em))

bind_rows(overall, stratified) %>%
  transmute(Group = Model, N,
            `Adjusted PR (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", Estimate, CI_Lower, CI_Upper))

c(Cochran_Q_p = p_Q, Wald_p = unname(p_wald), LRT_p = p_lrt) %>% round(2)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Writing up effect modification (Milestone 4)

*"We hypothesized a priori that the association between tree canopy and high blood pressure would
differ by gender, and we considered p < 0.10 from a test of interaction to indicate statistical
evidence of effect modification. Twenty-six non-binary participants were excluded from this analysis
because of small numbers. After adjustment for education and tract poverty, living in a top-quartile
canopy tract was associated with a lower prevalence of high blood pressure among men (PR = 0.62, 95%
CI: 0.45, 0.84) and, to a lesser extent, among women (PR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.62, 1.05). The
confidence intervals overlapped substantially, and tests of multiplicative interaction did not meet
our threshold (robust Wald p = 0.12; likelihood ratio test p = 0.14; Cochran's Q p = 0.19). We
therefore found limited statistical evidence that gender modifies this association, although the
difference in point estimates suggests a possibly stronger association among men that could be
examined in a larger study."*

Notice what the paragraph does: it states the hypothesis and threshold, reports **both** stratum
estimates with CIs, reports the actual p-values, and does not claim the association is "absent" in
women or "the same" in men and women.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 What if my modifier has more than two levels? Click to read"}
With a modifier that has $k$ levels (e.g., three education categories), the interaction model has
$k - 1$ interaction terms, and a test of effect modification needs to test them **all at once**.

- **Stratified models and Cochran's Q:** fit one model per level; Q has $k - 1$ degrees of freedom.
  The code in Step 6 works unchanged with more strata.
- **LRT:** compare the reduced and full models as in Step 10. `anova()` calculates the degrees of
  freedom ($k - 1$) automatically. This is the main reason the LRT is often preferred: it handles
  several interaction terms in one test.
- **Robust Wald test for several terms:** with modified Poisson, test all the interaction terms
  together using their robust variance-covariance matrix:

```r
int_terms <- grep(":", names(coef(model_int)), value = TRUE)   # all interaction terms
b <- coef(model_int)[int_terms]
V <- vcovHC(model_int, type = "HC0")[int_terms, int_terms]
wald_chisq <- as.numeric(t(b) %*% solve(V) %*% b)
pchisq(wald_chisq, df = length(b), lower.tail = FALSE)
```

Each level also needs enough exposed and unexposed participants **with and without the outcome**
(Step 2). If a level is too small, combine it with a similar level — and say why.

**Continuous modifiers** (e.g., age in years) can also go into an interaction term, but the
stratum-specific estimates then change with every unit of the modifier, which makes them harder to
present. For this course, use a categorical version of your modifier, with cut points chosen in
advance (e.g., ages < 50 vs. ≥ 50).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn: Effect modification in your own project"}
Using **your project's exposure, outcome, and final adjustment set** from Milestone 3:

1. Choose **one** potential effect modifier and write down your a priori hypothesis (which group do
   you expect to show the stronger association, and why?) and your p-value threshold — **before**
   running anything.
2. Code the modifier (0/1 if possible), check the modifier × exposure × outcome cell sizes, and
   create an analytic sample with no missing data on any model variable.
3. Fit your adjusted model within each stratum of the modifier, and make a table and plot of the
   stratum-specific estimates.
4. Fit the interaction model, and calculate Cochran's Q, the robust Wald test, and (if your
   log-binomial models converge) the LRT.
5. Write two or three sentences interpreting your results.
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — stratified estimates and tests of interaction for your own project

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Example: traffic density and asthma, by gender — click to reveal"}
Continuing the Lesson 6 example: the final model for high traffic density (above the median) and
asthma adjusted for tract poverty. *A priori hypothesis:* the association will differ by gender,
because asthma prevalence and its triggers differ between adult men and women. Threshold: p < 0.10.

```{webr-r}
data <- data %>%
  mutate(traffic_high = ifelse(ctb1traff > median(ctb1traff, na.rm = TRUE), 1, 0))

data_asthma <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(asthma), !is.na(traffic_high), !is.na(woman), !is.na(pov_allage))

# Cell sizes: gender x exposure x outcome
data_asthma %>% count(woman, traffic_high, asthma)

# Stratified models
m_men   <- glm(asthma ~ traffic_high + pov_allage, data = filter(data_asthma, woman == 0),
               family = poisson(link = "log"))
m_women <- glm(asthma ~ traffic_high + pov_allage, data = filter(data_asthma, woman == 1),
               family = poisson(link = "log"))

strat_asthma <- bind_rows(extract_ratio(m_men, "Men", robust = TRUE),
                          extract_ratio(m_women, "Women", robust = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(Term == "traffic_high")
strat_asthma %>% mutate(across(Estimate:CI_Upper, ~ round(.x, 2)))

# Cochran's Q
lp <- log(strat_asthma$Estimate)
s  <- (log(strat_asthma$CI_Upper) - log(strat_asthma$CI_Lower)) / 3.92
w  <- 1 / s^2
Q  <- sum(w * (lp - sum(w * lp) / sum(w))^2)

# Robust Wald test
m_int <- glm(asthma ~ traffic_high * woman + pov_allage, data = data_asthma,
             family = poisson(link = "log"))
V  <- vcovHC(m_int, type = "HC0")
z  <- coef(m_int)["traffic_high:woman"] / sqrt(V["traffic_high:woman", "traffic_high:woman"])

# LRT with log-binomial models
lb_reduced <- glm(asthma ~ traffic_high + woman + pov_allage, data = data_asthma,
                  family = binomial(link = "log"))
lb_full    <- glm(asthma ~ traffic_high * woman + pov_allage, data = data_asthma,
                  family = binomial(link = "log"))
lrt <- anova(lb_reduced, lb_full, test = "Chisq")

c(Q_p    = pchisq(Q, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE),
  Wald_p = unname(2 * pnorm(-abs(z))),
  LRT_p  = lrt$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]) %>% round(3)
```

After adjusting for tract poverty, living in a high-traffic tract was associated with a higher
prevalence of asthma among both men (PR = 1.40, 95% CI: 0.94, 2.08) and women (PR = 2.40, 95% CI:
1.60, 3.58). All three tests of interaction gave p-values between 0.06 and 0.07, below our
pre-specified threshold of 0.10, so there is statistical evidence that the traffic–asthma
association is stronger among women than among men on the multiplicative scale. Compare this with
the tree canopy example, where the difference between strata was smaller and the tests did not meet
the threshold.
:::

# Quick-Start Script for Your Own Project

::: {.callout-tip}
## 💻 In your RStudio script

```r
# ---- Setup ----
library(tidyverse)
library(sandwich)   # robust standard errors

# ---- Read in your processed data ----
data <- read.csv(file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"))

# ---- Helper: exponentiate coefficients and 95% CIs (robust = TRUE for modified Poisson) ----
extract_ratio <- function(model, label, robust = FALSE) {
  vc <- if (robust) vcovHC(model, type = "HC0") else vcov(model)
  b  <- coef(model)[-1]
  se <- sqrt(diag(vc))[-1]
  data.frame(Model = label, Term = names(b), Estimate = exp(b),
             CI_Lower = exp(b - 1.96 * se), CI_Upper = exp(b + 1.96 * se),
             row.names = NULL)
}

# ============================================================
# REPLACE: swap in your own variable names throughout
# A priori hypothesis: ...
# Threshold for evidence of effect modification: p < 0.10
# ============================================================

# ---- 1. Code the modifier (0/1) and check cell sizes ----
data <- data %>% mutate(MODIFIER = ...)          # e.g., case_when(...)
data %>% count(MODIFIER, YOUR_EXPOSURE, YOUR_OUTCOME)

# ---- 2. Analytic sample: no missing data on any model variable ----
data_em <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(YOUR_OUTCOME), !is.na(YOUR_EXPOSURE), !is.na(MODIFIER),
         !is.na(CONFOUNDER_1), !is.na(CONFOUNDER_2))

# ---- 3. Stratified models ----
m0 <- glm(YOUR_OUTCOME ~ YOUR_EXPOSURE + CONFOUNDER_1 + CONFOUNDER_2,
          data = filter(data_em, MODIFIER == 0), family = poisson(link = "log"))
m1 <- glm(YOUR_OUTCOME ~ YOUR_EXPOSURE + CONFOUNDER_1 + CONFOUNDER_2,
          data = filter(data_em, MODIFIER == 1), family = poisson(link = "log"))

stratified <- bind_rows(extract_ratio(m0, "Modifier = 0", robust = TRUE),
                        extract_ratio(m1, "Modifier = 1", robust = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(Term == "YOUR_EXPOSURE") %>%
  mutate(N = c(nobs(m0), nobs(m1)))
stratified

ggplot(stratified, aes(x = Model, y = Estimate, ymin = CI_Lower, ymax = CI_Upper)) +
  geom_pointrange() + geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() + labs(x = NULL, y = "Adjusted PR (95% CI), log scale") + theme_minimal()

# ---- 4. Cochran's Q ----
lp <- log(stratified$Estimate)
se <- (log(stratified$CI_Upper) - log(stratified$CI_Lower)) / 3.92
w  <- 1 / se^2
Q  <- sum(w * (lp - sum(w * lp) / sum(w))^2)
pchisq(Q, df = length(lp) - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

# ---- 5. Interaction model and robust Wald test ----
m_int <- glm(YOUR_OUTCOME ~ YOUR_EXPOSURE * MODIFIER + CONFOUNDER_1 + CONFOUNDER_2,
             data = data_em, family = poisson(link = "log"))
V <- vcovHC(m_int, type = "HC0")
b3 <- coef(m_int)["YOUR_EXPOSURE:MODIFIER"]
2 * pnorm(-abs(b3 / sqrt(V["YOUR_EXPOSURE:MODIFIER", "YOUR_EXPOSURE:MODIFIER"])))

# ---- 6. LRT with log-binomial models (same participants; nested) ----
lb_reduced <- glm(YOUR_OUTCOME ~ YOUR_EXPOSURE + MODIFIER + CONFOUNDER_1 + CONFOUNDER_2,
                  data = data_em, family = binomial(link = "log"))
lb_full    <- glm(YOUR_OUTCOME ~ YOUR_EXPOSURE * MODIFIER + CONFOUNDER_1 + CONFOUNDER_2,
                  data = data_em, family = binomial(link = "log"))
anova(lb_reduced, lb_full, test = "Chisq")
# If the log-binomial models don't converge, report the robust Wald test and Cochran's Q.
```
:::

# Wrap Up

This tutorial covered:

- The difference between confounding (a bias to remove) and effect modification (a finding to
  report), and why effect modification depends on the scale
- Stating an a priori hypothesis and a p-value threshold before looking at the data
- Coding a modifier and checking modifier × exposure × outcome cell sizes
- Stratified analysis: fitting the adjusted model within each stratum, plotting the estimates on a
  log scale, and comparing them qualitatively — and why "significant in one group but not the other"
  is not evidence of effect modification
- Cochran's Q, calculated on the log scale from stratum-specific estimates
- Interaction models: interpreting $\beta_1$, $\beta_3$, and $\beta_1 + \beta_3$; getting
  stratum-specific estimates and CIs; and keeping models hierarchical
- The robust Wald test and the likelihood ratio test for interaction, including why the LRT should
  use log-binomial rather than modified Poisson models, and why the models must be nested and fit
  in the same participants

The stratified table and tests you produced for your own project are a first draft of
**Milestone 4** and of **Table 3** in your final report.

**Next week:** Reproducible epidemiologic analysis and using AI to support analyses — you'll organize
your project code so that someone else (or future you) can rerun everything from start to finish.
